title: Microvascular Leakage in Hemorrhagic Shock and Trauma
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it is designed to produce preclinical groundwork for
new strategies to reduce elevations in microvascular permeability that worsen outcomes of traumatic injury.
The project is relevant to the part of the NIH mission that pertains to developing fundamental knowledge that
will help prevent disability and early loss of life.

title: Antimicrobial Biomaterials that Interfere with Bacterial Nucleotide Messenger Signaling
text:
Bacterial intracellular nucleotide second messenger signaling plays an important role in biofilm development.
The project proposes to develop small molecules and tether these molecules on polymeric biomaterial
surfaces so that small molecules can interfere with nucleotide signaling pathways and interrupt biofilm
formation and growth on biomaterial surfaces, and will increase the efficacy of antibiotics against biofilm
bacteria in vitro and in vivo.

title: Core C: Biostatistics and Data Management
text:
The Biostatistics and Data Management Core (Core C) will ensure that the appropriate design is incorporated 
into all SPORE studies from inception, that data are appropriately validated, linked, cleaned, and analyzed, and 
that all results will be interpreted for statistical as well as biological and clinical significance. The Core will develop 
and maintain an integrated database environment for efficient data management, integration, analysis, and 
sharing for all SPORE projects and investigators.

title: Determining the effects of imprinting on the humoral response induced by H5N1 influenza vaccines
text:
Highly pathogenic avian H5N1 influenza A viruses continue to spread across wildlife and agricultural animals in
the United States, increasing the risk of zoonotic adaptation and necessitating effective vaccine development.
This research project aims to define how immune imprinting shapes H5N1 vaccine responses and identify
antigen design strategies that overcome imprinting to maximize vaccine-induced protective antibodies and
durable B cell memory. These insights will strengthen pandemic preparedness efforts and mitigate morbidity,
mortality, and transmission during future influenza threats.

title: Determining the Role of Distinct Parafascicular Thalamic Circuits in Motor Behaviors Relevant to Parkinson’s Disease
text:
Motor impairments are among the most debilitating symptoms in a wide range of neurodegenerative disorders,
including Parkinson's disease. This project will determine the role of distinct subpopulations of neurons in
parafascicular (PF) thalamus in regulating locomotion and motor learning processes, which are commonly
disrupted in movement disorders. By characterizing the dysfunction of PF subpopulations in a mouse model of
Parkinson's disease, this project will identify PF circuit manipulations capable of treating multiple motor
phenotypes.

title: CRCNS: Decision dynamics in cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic networks
text:
Dysfunction in how the brain uses feedback to guide future decisions is a primary mechanism for many
public health problems (e.g., addiction). This research program will provide new insights into how neural
circuits give rise to decision-making and how environmental contexts (e.g., dynamic continuous and
discrete actions) regulate brain network configurations to produce behavioral flexibility, providing key
insights into the neural systems that give rise to addictive behaviors and other public health problems.

title: Unraveling the Molecular Basis of Tooth Agenesis
text:
Tooth agenesis (TA) affects approximately 200 million people worldwide, making it one of the most prevalent
craniofacial anomalies in humans, and for which no cure or prevention is known. This project will identify causal
TA genes/variants and characterize the effects of their dysregulation on gene/protein function and additional
health outcomes. The results will improve understanding of the genetic basis of TA and translate to clinical care
with improved characterization and informed strategies towards tooth-replacement modalities.

title: Cellular mechanisms of palatal shelf outgrowth
text:
Craniofacial anomalies make up around one-third of all birth defects, and cleft palate occurs in greater than one
out of every 1500 live births. During secondary palate morphogenesis, complex cell movement within the
heterogeneous palatal mesenchyme is essential, but how this movement is regulated remains unclear. This
proposal aims to address this gap using state-of-the-art approaches and new tools for studying cellular
movement during morphogenesis in mammalian craniofacial development with the ultimate goal of advancing
therapeutic treatments.

title: Cancer Genetics Professional Education in a Global Community of Practice
text:
To help address the significant global demand for cancer genomics education, skills development and
evidence-based patient care, this project proposes to continue a successful, multifaceted Intensive Course and
global Clinical Cancer Genomics Community of Practice. The program leverages the expertise and resources
of the academic center to prepare community-based clinicians with the knowledge and skills needed to
integrate genomic advances into best practices in cancer risk assessment, personalized risk management and
targeted cancer treatment. Fulfillment of the activities outlined in this proposal will further our efforts to grow the
number of clinicians with practitioner-level proficiency in genetic cancer genetics across the U.S. and
internationally.

title: Epithelial cell mediated fibroblast activation through CTHRC1-TGFb signaling in fibrotic lung diseases
text:
Fibrotic lung diseases represent a heterogeneous group of diseases that arise from a variety of
genetic defects, immune conditions, or inhalational exposures. The molecular mechanisms
contributing to fibrosis remain unclear, and new therapeutic approaches remain a critical unmet
clinical need. Supported by novel preliminary data from human explanted lungs, we propose to
investigate CTHRC1 and its downstream targets as a promising new therapeutic target to prevent
or treat fibrosis of both the lung airways and parenchyma.

title: Mapping Trajectories of Alzheimer's Progression via Personalized Brain Anchor-nodes
text:
Leveraging four publicly available large-scale neuroimaging datasets, this project aims to improve personalized
early diagnosis and prediction of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) by constructing reliable, corresponding and
individualized imaging measures based on brain landmarks and by representing the continuum of AD
progression based on these features.

title: A flexible, low power, multi-channel, real-time BCI for seizure monitoring and Modulation
text:
Over 3 million people in the United States suffer from epilepsy, which is a serious disease that in many cases
cannot be effectively treated with medications or brain surgery. The goal of this project is to develop and test a
powerful new processor and supporting software to analyze brain signals in a brain implantable
neuromodulation device for epilepsy. We believe this project will result in both an improved understanding of
epilepsy and improved therapy for epilepsy and is thus highly relevant to the NINDS mission to reduce the
burden of neurological disease.

title: Dissecting the mechanisms of HIV resistance in vivo to broadly neutralizing antibodies
text:
Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) against HIV-1 provide new opportunities for immunotherapy and
prevention but the development of HIV-1 resistance to bnAbs is still an obstacle for medical interventions. Here
we will study how HIV-1 strains resist multiple bnAbs and investigate indirect pathways that HIV-1 may use to
escape bnAbs. We will define new ways to overcome HIV-1 resistance to bnAbs and provide important insights
into the interactions of HIV-1 and bnAbs.

title: Characterization and Digital Phenotyping of Migraine and Affective Disorders during Hormonal Fluctuations across the Life Course
text:
During hormonally active periods, individuals are at greater risk of affective disorders, particularly if they
experience comorbid migraine. The proposed research aims to evaluate migraineurs as a unique phenotype of
individuals with affective disorders due to their vulnerability to hormonal fluctuations using passive and
ecological momentary assessment smartphone data. This project will enhance prospective cohort data
collection of episodic conditions and improve mental health risk assessment, screening, and treatment for
migraineurs, those suffering from affective disorders, and those with this common comorbidity.

title: Dissecting the role of gut microbial-derived metabolites on epilepsy
text:
Despite the emergence of new antiepileptic drug options, there is a consistent proportion of epilepsy patients
that remain drug-resistant. This proposal takes an innovative approach by studying the role of the gut microbiota
and its metabolites on seizure occurrence and neuronal physiology. We will examine a microbial-derived
metabolite as a key factor in seizure development, which will provide a basis for investigating its role as a
therapeutic target in epilepsy.

title: MATCHMAKERS - Solving T-cell receptor recognition and design via integrated high-throughput screening and structural, functional and computational approaches
text: UCSF Understanding how T cell receptors (TCRs) see tumor antigens presented by MHCs is necessary to fully understand how the immune system recognizes tumor antigens, and to reap the full potential of antigen-specific immunotherapy. To achieve this goal, a quantum leap forward is required in which the revolutionary advances in machine learning are combined with a large volume of structure, function, data on matched TCR-pMHC pairs. The development of accurate predictors of TCR-antigen recognition will be dependent on the creation and integration sequencing-based datasets with high-throughput structural and functional insights. Our proposal, submitted as a CRUK/NCI Grand Challenge team (MATCHMAKERS) will combine researchers with expertise in immunology, methods development, structural biology, and computation to enable generalized prediction and design of TCR recognition. This work will be spread across four Work Packages (WPs): WP1: Large-scale generation of TCR-pMHC pairs from naturally occurring sources. We will build datasets of naturally occurring TCR-pMHC pairs. Our team will use an array of approaches to collect these datasets, from humans and from mouse models, and in the context of both cancer and immunity more generally. WP2: Ultra-high throughput TCR-pMHC matching using molecular engineering. Efforts to create general models will require a broader array of data than feasible to collect from natural TCR systems. We will use an array of synthetic approaches developed by our team to comprehensively match TCRs with pMHCs to train computational models. WP3: Large-scale structural and biochemical analyses of TCR-pMHC interactions. A key to our team’s vision is to match interaction datasets with high throughput structural and functional insights. A deep understanding of how the TCR contacts with MHC helices control function and orientation will be essential for training and testing computational models. WP4 AI-based prediction and design of TCR-pMHC interactions. We will integrate our data to train next- generation algorithms capable of generally predicting and designing TCR-pMHC interactions. These predictions will proceed through a reiterative testing and feedback circuits for further model optimization.

title: Small Molecule Inhibitors of Nef-Mediated Immune Evasion
text:
Current antiretrovirals can control the HIV-1 infections but cannot cure the disease. In this project, we will de-
velop novel antiretrovirals targeting the Nef protein of the HIV-1 virus. Such drugs, once developed, should
empower host immune cells, which are otherwise suppressed by Nef, to find and kill infected cells possibly
leading to a cure.

title: Structure-guided functional analysis of GluA4-NPTX2 interaction during PVIN homeostatic scaling
text:
This project is relevant to human health because it will combine structural biology and biophysics with
conventional cellular neuroscience techniques to test a key hypothesis about how neurotransmitter receptor
organization regulates synaptic strength, plasticity, and human disease states. In the future, the detailed
structural and functional understanding of glutamate receptor clustering that results from this work will inform
the design of therapeutics for targeting the organization of glutamate receptors. Therefore, the proposed
research is relevant to the NIH mission of protecting and improving human health by understanding the
processes that control synaptic neurotransmitter receptor regulation in unprecedented detail.

title: Effects of Stress on Brain and Physiological Pathways to Health Disparities
text: Stress is a continued threat to public health and a contributor to major adverse health outcomes like depression, anxiety and traumatic stress disorders, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes. Although empirical research has begun to examine the brain and physiological pathways linking stress to these adverse health conditions, few studies have examined how stress affects these pathways in diverse populations, particularly those disproportionately exposed to stressors. The proposed research will examine the effects of personal experiences with a variety of stressors on the brain, mind, and body in a diverse sample, and will determine how these changes associate with adverse health outcomes.

title: Experimental Therapeutics Program
text: 10.0 Abstract: Experimental Therapeutics (ET) Program The overarching goal of ET is to develop and test new therapies for solid tumors and hematologic malignancies based on innovative preclinical research. The emphasis is on bringing basic and preclinical discoveries from ET members to early-stage clinical testing and also on providing platforms for investigators in other programs to evaluate their findings in clinical settings. To achieve this mission, the program focuses on three specific aims: Aim 1: Target detection and measurement—Investigate diagnostic advances, including molecular early detection, liquid biopsy and imaging, to guide new treatment approaches and assessments of response; Aim 2: Molecular targeting: Development and preclinical and clinical testing—Investigate new cancer therapies based on novel molecular targets in in vitro and in vivo laboratory studies as well as early phase clinical trials; and Aim 3: Treatment delivery: Novel delivery strategies—Investigate the development of new technologies for therapy delivery, including molecular carriers, nanotechnology, and novel radiation therapy and radiation protection approaches. To achieve these three aims, members of ET are supported by extensive expertise available in other University of Maryland Marlene and Stewart Greenebaum Comprehensive Cancer Center (UMGCCC) Programs to translate basic research findings to the clinic and by the availability of exceptional shared services. The ET Program has 56 members, including 31 full members and 25 associate members, who conduct cancer-focused research that receives $14.6 million direct cost annual funding ($19.4 million total), including $3.6 million (25%) from NCI and $4.1 million from other peer-reviewed sources. ET Program members receive $6.9 million annually from non-peer-reviewed funding sources. During this funding period, ET members authored 889 cancer-related publications, of which 22% resulted from intraprogrammatic, 21% from interprogrammatic, and 8% from intra- and interprogrammatic collaborations. Of the 889 publications, 72% include collaborations with external investigators, reflecting the high national impact of the ET Program. A high percentage of ET publications (14%) were in journals with an impact factor ≥10. Research efforts of ET members are supported by extensive use of all shared services. The ET Program collaborates with the other four UMGCCC research programs and facilitate community outreach and engagement (COE) to identify and address the cancer research priorities of the catchment area.
